```{r}
library(tidyverse)
stat113_df <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/highamm/ds234_quarto/main/data_online/stat113.csv")
```

## Section 2.3: Introduction to Plotting

One quantitative variable.

```{r}
stat113_df
ggplot(data = stat113_df, aes(x = GPA)) +
  geom_histogram(colour = "navyblue", fill = "plum2", bins = 15)

ggplot(data = stat113_df, aes(x = GPA)) +
  geom_freqpoly(bins = 17)

ggplot(data = stat113_df, aes(x = GPA)) +
    geom_histogram(colour = "black", fill = "white", bins = 17) +
    geom_freqpoly(bins = 17)
```

One categorical variable.

```{r}
ggplot(data = stat113_df, aes(x = Award)) +
  geom_bar(colour = "mistyrose", fill = "lightcoral")
```

Two categorical variables.

```{r}
ggplot(data = stat113_df, aes(x = Sport, fill = SocialMedia)) +
  geom_bar() 

ggplot(data = stat113_df, aes(x = Sport, fill = Award)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(y = "Proportion")
```

One categorical and one quantitative

```{r}
ggplot(data = stat113_df, aes(x = Award, y = Exercise)) +
  geom_boxplot()

ggplot(data = stat113_df, aes(x = Sex, y = GPA)) +
  geom_violin(colour = "slategrey", fill = "yellow")
## there no evidence of association between sex and gpa

ggplot(data = stat113_df, aes(x = Award, y = Exercise)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.10)
## the strip plot shows a rough idea of sample size
```
